tagline: The story of how Israel moved from judges to kings, told through three lives: Samuel the prophet, Saul the first king, and David the shepherd God chose to replace him.
overview:
First Samuel opens in the last dark years of the judges, with a childless woman praying at the shrine of Shiloh, and closes on a battlefield where Israel's first king falls on his own sword. In between, the nation changes shape. Samuel, the answer to Hannah's prayer, grows up to be prophet, priest, and the last of the judges. The ark of the covenant is captured by the Philistines and comes home again without any human hero. The people ask for a king like the nations, and God, though he calls the request a rejection of himself, gives them Saul. Saul begins well and unravels, and the second half of the book follows David, anointed in secret as a boy, as he rises in Saul's court, flees Saul's jealousy, and waits in the wilderness for a throne he refuses to seize.

The book is about power: who holds it, how it is given, and what it does to the people who hold it. Its great refrain is that the LORD raises up and brings down, a theme sung in Hannah's prayer at the start and worked out in every life that follows. Eli's house falls, Samuel rises; Saul is chosen and then rejected; David, the youngest son left out with the sheep, is chosen because God looks past appearances. First Samuel is also where the Bible first attaches the word anointed, messiah, to a king, which makes it the ground on which the later hope for a Messiah is built.

In the Hebrew Bible, First and Second Samuel are one book. The Greek translation made by Jews before the time of Jesus (the Septuagint) divided it in two and grouped it with Kings as the four books of the Kingdoms, and printed Hebrew Bibles later followed the two-part division. Reading 1 Samuel well means remembering that its story does not stop at chapter 31.
author:
The book is anonymous. It can't have been written by Samuel in its finished form, since he dies in 1 Samuel 25 and the story continues well past him. A Jewish tradition preserved in the Babylonian Talmud credits Samuel with the book and says the prophets Gad and Nathan completed it, a view that draws on 1 Chronicles 29:29, which mentions records kept by Samuel the seer, Nathan the prophet, and Gad the seer. Many readers take that verse as evidence that written prophetic sources lay behind the book, whoever gave it its final shape.

Modern scholars generally see the book as a compilation of earlier accounts. Leonhard Rost, in the 1920s, argued for an older ark narrative (roughly 1 Samuel 4 to 6 with part of 2 Samuel 6) and a separate account of the succession to David's throne; many also identify a history of David's rise (roughly 1 Samuel 16 to 2 Samuel 5). Since Martin Noth's work in 1943, many have read Samuel as part of a larger Deuteronomistic History running from Deuteronomy through Kings, shaped by the theology of Deuteronomy and brought to final form around the time of the Babylonian exile. More conservative scholars stress the book's unity of theme and its early, eyewitness-like detail, and see prophetic writers close to the events as its main authors. All agree the book is carefully composed, whatever its sources.
date:
The events run from the birth of Samuel to the death of Saul, roughly the second half of the eleventh century BC. Saul's reign is usually placed around 1050 to 1010 BC and David's accession around 1010 BC, though these figures are approximate and 1 Samuel 13:1 has a damaged number in the Hebrew text for the length of Saul's reign.

The writing is later than the events. The note in 1 Samuel 27:6 that Ziklag has belonged to the kings of Judah to this day assumes a time when there were separate kings of Judah, which points to after the kingdom divided around 930 BC. Scholars who read Samuel as part of the Deuteronomistic History date its final edition to the late seventh or the sixth century BC, while allowing that its sources are much older. Others place the bulk of the book within a century or two of David. The Dead Sea Scrolls include several manuscripts of Samuel (the best known is called 4QSamuel-a), and in a number of places their wording agrees with the Septuagint against the standard Hebrew text, which shows that the book circulated in more than one form in the centuries before Christ.
setting:
Israel at the start of the book is a loose federation of tribes in the central hill country, without a capital, a standing army, or a king. Its main shrine is at Shiloh, in the territory of Ephraim, where the ark of the covenant is kept under the care of Eli's family. The greatest threat comes from the Philistines, a people who had settled on the southern coastal plain in the early twelfth century BC as part of the wider movement of the Sea Peoples. They were organized in five city-states (Gaza, Ashkelon, Ashdod, Gath, and Ekron), each ruled by a lord, and they pressed steadily up into the hills. Other pressures came from the Ammonites east of the Jordan and the Amalekites in the southern desert.

The great empires of Egypt and Mesopotamia were weak in this period, which left room for small kingdoms to form across Canaan and the lands east of the Jordan. Israel's demand for a king in 1 Samuel 8 happens in that world, where kingship was the normal form of government and where a war leader who could unite the tribes against the Philistines looked like the obvious answer to Israel's troubles.
purpose:
The book explains how Israel came to have kings, and why the throne passed from Saul's house to David's. It defends David's right to rule: again and again it shows him refusing to harm Saul, the LORD's anointed, and it shows that he rose because God chose him, not because he grasped. It also weighs kingship itself. The book is honest that the request for a king was a failure of trust (1 Samuel 8:7 has the LORD say “they have rejected Me as their king”), and yet God takes up the institution and makes it a vehicle of his promise.

For readers in any period, and especially for those who first read the finished book after the monarchy had failed and Jerusalem had fallen, 1 Samuel asks what kind of leader God's people should want and what kind of heart God looks for. It teaches that obedience matters more than ritual, that God keeps his word against the powerful, and that he can raise the lowly when all human options have run out.
story: First Samuel picks up where Judges leaves off, in a time when there was no king in Israel and everyone did what was right in their own eyes. The book of Ruth, placed just before it in Christian Bibles, ends with the name David, so a reader comes to 1 Samuel already waiting for him. The book carries Israel from the last judge to the first kings. Second Samuel continues directly with David's reign, and 1 and 2 Kings follow the royal line from Solomon to the fall of Jerusalem. The promise God makes to David in 2 Samuel 7, of a son whose throne will last forever, rests on the choice of David made in this book.
christ:
Hannah's song closes with the hope that the LORD will “exalt the horn of His anointed” (1 Samuel 2:10), the first time in the Bible that the word anointed (in Hebrew mashiach, the root of messiah) refers to a king. In 1 Samuel the anointed is Saul and then David, but the word becomes the name of Israel's hope for a coming king, and the New Testament calls Jesus the Christ, the Greek translation of that title. Mary's song in Luke 1 echoes Hannah's closely: God scatters the proud, brings down rulers, lifts the humble, and fills the hungry.

David's story also sets a pattern the Gospels draw on. He is anointed long before he reigns, rejected and hunted by the ruling power, surrounded by the distressed and the outcast, and he refuses to take the kingdom by force. Paul, preaching in Acts 13, moves from Saul to David to Jesus as the Savior God brought from David's line. The connection is a matter of promise and pattern: 1 Samuel does not predict Jesus in detail, but it gives the words, anointed king and son of David, in which the church confessed him.
reading:
First Samuel is narrative history, told with a novelist's skill and a prophet's judgment. The narrator rarely comments directly; meaning comes through dialogue, repetition, and contrast between characters (Hannah and Peninnah, Samuel and Eli's sons, Saul and David). Watch for the reversals Hannah's song announces and for the recurring language of seeing, hearing, and the heart. Speeches, especially those of Samuel in chapters 8, 12, and 15, often state the book's theology outright.

A few misreadings are common. The book is not a set of moral examples in which every hero is to be copied; David's flaws are on display even here, and Saul is tragic as well as guilty. Not every event is approved by being reported. Some passages also seem to tell the same story twice (Saul meets David in both chapter 16 and chapter 17, and David spares Saul twice in chapters 24 and 26). Scholars debate whether these reflect combined sources, deliberate retelling, or events that really happened more than once; a reader can notice the pattern without deciding that question.

structure.title: Samuel's birth and call
structure.summary: Hannah prays for a son and gives him to the LORD at Shiloh. While Eli's sons corrupt the priesthood, the boy Samuel hears God's word and becomes a recognized prophet.

structure.title: The ark lost and returned
structure.summary: Israel is defeated by the Philistines, the ark is captured, and Eli's house falls. The ark humbles the Philistine god Dagon and returns to Israel, and Samuel leads the people in repentance and victory.

structure.title: Israel asks for a king
structure.summary: The people demand a king like the nations. Samuel warns them, then anoints Saul, who is chosen by lot, proves himself against the Ammonites, and is confirmed as king while Samuel calls the nation to faithfulness.

structure.title: Saul's reign and rejection
structure.summary: Saul wins battles but disobeys the LORD's commands, and Samuel announces that the kingdom will be given to another.

structure.title: David at Saul's court
structure.summary: David is anointed in secret, defeats Goliath, and wins the love of Jonathan and the people, while Saul's jealousy turns murderous.

structure.title: David the fugitive
structure.summary: David flees into the wilderness, gathers a band of followers, twice spares Saul's life, and finally takes refuge among the Philistines.

structure.title: The end of Saul
structure.summary: Saul consults a medium at Endor, David is kept from fighting against Israel, and Saul and his sons die on Mount Gilboa.

themes.title: God raises the lowly and brings down the proud
themes.body: Hannah's song announces the book's pattern: the barren bear children, the hungry are fed, the mighty are broken, and the LORD lifts the poor from the ash heap. The story then acts it out. Eli's house falls while the child of a humiliated woman rises; the ark is captured and yet brings a proud god face down; the tall king is set aside for the youngest son. Power in this book is always given, and it can be taken back.

themes.title: Kingship under God
themes.body: The book treats kingship with deep ambivalence. Asking for a king is called a rejection of the LORD, and Samuel lists what a king will take from them. Yet God gives the king, chooses him, and later makes the throne of David the carrier of his promises. The question is never simply whether Israel should have a king, but whether the king will rule as a servant under the word of God. Saul fails that test; David, for all his faults, is shown as a man whose heart is turned toward God.

themes.title: The word of the LORD
themes.body: The book begins when the word of the LORD was rare and quickly becomes a story about a prophet through whom God speaks. Samuel anoints kings and rebukes them, and the kings stand or fall by whether they listen. The emphasis is on hearing and obeying, above sacrifice and ritual, which the book treats as worthless when used to manipulate God (as with the ark in chapter 4) or to cover disobedience.

themes.title: The heart and appearances
themes.body: People in 1 Samuel keep judging by what they can see: Eli misreads Hannah's prayer as drunkenness, Israel wants a king who looks like a king, and Samuel himself is impressed by the height of Jesse's oldest son. God repeatedly looks elsewhere. Saul is head and shoulders above everyone, and the story shows that stature is not character. David is chosen from the sheepfold.

themes.title: Loyalty and friendship
themes.body: The Hebrew word hesed, loyal and covenant-keeping love, shapes some of the book's finest scenes, especially the friendship between David and Jonathan, Saul's son and heir, who gives up his claim to the throne out of love for David and trust in God's choice. Loyalty is tested throughout: to God, to his anointed, to friends, and to promises.

keyChapters.why: Hannah's song sets out the book's theology of reversal and names the LORD's anointed king for the first time, while Eli's house is condemned.
The LORD calls the boy Samuel, and the word of God returns to Israel through a prophet.
The ark is captured and the glory departs from Israel, a disaster that shows God cannot be used as a weapon.
Israel asks for a king like the nations, and God grants the request while calling it a rejection of his own rule.
Saul disobeys, and Samuel announces that obedience is better than sacrifice and that the kingdom has been torn from him.
David is anointed, because the LORD looks at the heart, and the Spirit leaves Saul.
David defeats Goliath, trusting in the LORD's name rather than in weapons.
David spares Saul in the cave, refusing to lift his hand against the LORD's anointed.
